title: Pure Land, closed
hookLine: a vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light

lines: A SUNSET. A LAND OF LIGHT.
cards: A vow. A name. A sunset.
A land of light. If the Pure Land fit on a postcard, those four would be the picture. A monk long ago makes vows so large they need a whole world to hold them.

A buddha's name becomes something anyone can say: a farmer, a queen in prison, a clog-maker at his bench. The sun goes down in the west like a drum hung in the sky. And beyond it lies a land where even the birds teach.

teach.b: First, the vow. It began with Sukhavati, the land of bliss, and the monk Dharmakara, who in the Larger Sukhavati-vyuha makes his great vows.

At their heart is the primal vow: that anyone who calls his name with trust will be born in his land. Dharmakara becomes Amitabha, the Buddha of infinite light and infinite life. Second, the land and the seeing.
The Smaller sutra described the jeweled trees and the birds that teach.

Then Queen Vaidehi, locked away by her own son, asked for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha taught her to see it: the setting sun, then water, ice and crystal ground. Third, the name: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo.

Tanluan and Shandao shaped the practice in China. In Japan, Shinran spoke of other power, tariki, and of shinjin, true entrusting, with the name said in gratitude. Rennyo carried it to farmers in simple letters.
In China and Vietnam, people sit and call the name together. At the deathbed, the name is said with the dying. And the myokonin, like Saichi the clog-maker, lived it with quiet joy.

teach.h: THE LAND: TREES, BIRDS, A SETTING SUN.
teach.b: Fourth, the land today: temples far from Asia, some called churches; teachers who say the land is also a mind made pure here; and more than one answer about what the land is, held side by side.

teach.h: THE NAME: SAID IN TRUST AND THANKS.
teach.b: What runs through all of it is light.

teach.h: THE LAND TODAY: HERE, THERE, BOTH.
teach.b: Amitabha's name means infinite light, and the tradition holds that this light leaves no one out.
Tomorrow a new part begins: the traditions of Tibet.

how: Pure Land Buddhists call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan and Namo Amituofo in China, in temple services, at home, with the dying, and in gratitude, trusting the vow of a Buddha of infinite light.

o: Amitabha's tradition: a vow, a name and a land of light
a monastery rule to keep the temple grounds spotless
a Zen garden of raked sand, meant for still sitting

games.q: Pure Land, closed: tap the pairs.
p: the monk who made the vows
asked for a land without sorrow

s: he is the Buddha of infinite light and infinite life.
the Pure Land path is only for monks
the name is for anyone: a queen, a farmer, a clog-maker.
all Pure Land teachers describe the land the same way
some say a real land, some say the mind made pure, some say both.

games.q: you're Queen Vaidehi, locked away by your own son. the Buddha comes to you. what do you ask for?
games.why: she asks for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha teaches her to see it, starting with the setting sun.

practice: If you say the nembutsu, say it now, once or a few times, Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo, slowly, and then stop; if you don't, hold the words infinite light in mind for one breath.
Then rest, and let the light, whatever it means to you, do the rest of the sitting.

wordCard.voice: Pure Land. The tradition of Amitabha Buddha: a vow, a name said with trust, a land of light in the west and, for some teachers, a mind made pure here. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Amitabha, infinite light. in Japan, Amida; in China, Amituo.

carryVoice: Your line: infinite light. A vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light. That's the Pure Land, whole.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavati-vyuha (Dharmakara's vows; the primal vow)
Amitayur-dhyana Sutra (Vaidehi; the setting sun, water and ice)
